healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Hungary. Emergency numbers (104/107/105/112), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, travel insurance advice, and vaccination recommendations.

recommended: tick-borne encephalitis (if spending time outdoors in forested areas)
vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers. Ensure routine vaccinations are current. Tick-borne encephalitis is present in some forested areas — vaccination recommended for hikers and outdoor enthusiasts.

pharmacy.hours: Most pharmacies open Mon-Fri 8am-6pm, Sat 8am-2pm. Some 24/7 pharmacies in Budapest and major cities. Look for 'Patika' signs. Green cross = pharmacy.
pharmacy.tips: Pharmacists in Budapest and tourist areas often speak English and German. Many OTC medications are available. EU prescriptions are accepted. Hungary has a strong pharmaceutical manufacturing sector — generic medications are widely available and affordable.

water.notes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Hungary, including Budapest. Hungarian tap water is of good quality and regularly tested.

healthcare.foodSafetyTips: Hungary has good food safety standards. Traditional dishes like goulash (pörkölt), lángos, and stuffed peppers (töltött paprika) are generally safe. Hungarian paprika is famous — buy from reputable sources. Be cautious with unfamiliar wild foods.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not required but strongly recommended for all travelers.
travelInsurance.tips: Hungary is very affordable for medical care — dental work, optical care, and general medical consultations cost a fraction of Western Europe. Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is still recommended for serious emergencies. Budapest has many private clinics that cater to medical tourists.

healthcare.qualityNotes: Good healthcare infrastructure, especially in Budapest which has modern private clinics with English-speaking staff. Public hospitals are adequate but may have longer waits and less English. Dental care is a particular strength — Hungary is one of Europe's top dental tourism destinations. Pharmacies are widely available.

medications.generalAdvice: Hungary follows EU/Schengen rules for medication imports. EU prescriptions are accepted, while non-EU prescriptions require re-issuing by a Hungarian doctor. For controlled substances, travelers from Schengen countries need a Schengen medical certificate. Hungary's OGYÉI (National Institute of Pharmacy and Nutrition) oversees medication regulation.

controlledSubstances.note: Cannabis is illegal in Hungary with zero tolerance. Even small amounts can lead to criminal prosecution. CBD products with 0% THC are legal but products with any THC are illegal. Do not bring any cannabis or THC products — Hungary has some of the strictest cannabis laws in the EU.
Controlled under Hungarian narcotics law. Requires Schengen certificate or doctor's letter. Carry only personal-use quantities in original packaging.
Strictly controlled. Requires documentation and Schengen certificate. Contact Hungarian health authorities before travel if you need to bring ADHD medications.
Controlled. EU regulations apply. Carry Schengen certificate, doctor's letter, and original packaging. Hungarian customs may check quantities.
Hungary has comprehensive bans on new psychoactive substances. Possession and import carry severe criminal penalties.

connectivity.simOptions: Telekom, Telenor (Yettel), or Vodafone prepaid SIMs at Budapest airport or city shops. EU roaming with any EU SIM.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at most cafes (Budapest's café culture is strong), hotels, and thermal baths. Good 4G coverage citywide.
connectivity.bestOption: EU SIM with roaming. Otherwise Vodafone prepaid at airport. eSIM via Airalo as quick alternative.

cultural.tipping: 10-15% at restaurants (specify when paying — don't leave on table). Round up for taxis. Tip thermal bath attendants HUF 500-1000.
cultural.dressCode: Smart casual in Budapest. Business dress is formal. Bring swimwear for thermal baths (some require swim caps).
cultural.greetings: Handshake with eye contact. 'Szia' (see-ah) for casual hello. Hungarians put surname first (like Japanese). Close friends may cheek-kiss.
taboos: Clinking beer glasses (relates to 1848 Austrian celebration — some Hungarians still observe this)
Confusing Hungary with other Eastern European countries
Not taking off shoes when entering someone's home
cultural.haggling: Not practiced at shops or restaurants. The Great Market Hall has fixed prices despite being touristy. Watch for tourist-trap restaurants in Váci utca.

safety.lgbtSafety: Hungary has become increasingly hostile to LGBTQ+ rights under recent legislation that restricts LGBTQ+ content in media and schools. Budapest still has a visible LGBTQ+ scene and hosts Pride events, but the political climate is unwelcoming. Exercise caution outside the capital.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Hungary is generally safe for solo female travelers. Budapest is well-traveled and public transport is reliable. Be cautious in the party district (District VII) late at night and watch drinks at ruin bars — drink spiking has been reported.
safety.notes: Hungary is a safe destination with low violent crime. Pickpocketing is the main concern in Budapest, particularly on trams 4/6, at Keleti station, and in crowded tourist areas. Taxi overcharging is common — always use Bolt or pre-booked taxis rather than hailing on the street.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free (Schengen). UK, EU, Australia, Canada, Japan also visa-free.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-June and September-October (mild, fewer crowds). July-August (hot, festivals). December for Christmas markets and thermal baths.

hospitals.name: Semmelweis University Hospital
hospitals.notes: Major university hospital in Budapest. Some English-speaking doctors.

hospitals.name: Privatklinik Rózsakerti
hospitals.notes: Private clinic catering to foreigners. English-speaking staff, accepts international insurance.

immediate: Follow Országos Katasztrófavédelmi Főigazgatóság (OKF) flood alerts
Move to higher ground if near Danube or Tisza river during flood warnings
Do not drive through flooded roads
after: Report flood damage to local municipality
Monitor OKF website for situation updates
resources: National Directorate General for Disaster Management (OKF): www.katasztrofavedelem.hu | 112

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 107)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (107) and ambulance (104) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.
